chapter_theme: Poverty (நல்குரவு) strips a man of livelihood, kin and standing; but the deeper want is a pit that goods cannot fill, filled only when impurity is gone, by praising the Lord and lighting the lamp of awareness.
structure_note: 209 describes worldly poverty; 210 and 211 turn it into the unfillable pit; 212 and 213 move from kin and the five senses to seeking the Lord.

209.reading: The cloth is torn, the living is gone, even those who depended on him have turned unloving; for those who drift about the land there is no giving, no receiving, no festivity and no standing.
209.nuance: கோள் is taken as receiving, so the poor man is cut out of exchange both ways. நடை may be gait, standing or custom; I read it as standing among others.

210.reading: You who, as each dawn breaks, hunt for scarce goods to fill the false pit, praise the Lord whatever pit you fill; that pit is filled only when impurity is gone.
210.nuance: பொய்க்குழி, the false pit, is traditionally the belly, filled each day and empty again; it can also be read as the want that the body and its desires make. அழுக்கு is taken as the soul's impurity (மலம்). Both a plain and a spiritual reading of the pit stand.

211.reading: People seek even gold to fill the stony pit, and no one finds that easy; once one knows the understanding that fills it, the pit fills as impurity leaves.
211.nuance: கற்குழி may be a pit dug in rock, so hard to fill, or a play on கல்வி. The verse repeats 210 but names knowledge rather than praise as the way.

212.reading: The kin who cling and follow are worse than one's deeds; before the life departs, light the lamp of awareness while in the body, keep to it, and that road can be closed.
212.nuance: அவ்வழி may be the pit of 210 and 211 or the road of rebirth; கடந்தோர் in the second line is hard to construe. The claim that kin are worse than வினை is striking: kin hold one to the world as deeds do.

213.reading: The five senses, roaming like cattle over the paths, have inflicted endless suffering, and strong deeds have struck again and again; weary of such a life, he stood asking for the Lord.
213.nuance: The first line is obscure: அறுத்தன ஆறினும் ஆனினம் மேவி may be cattle grazing in cleared fields or on the six paths. ஐவர், 'the five', is traditionally the senses. The chapter's poverty here becomes the soul's.

links.note: Both say kin and dependants fall away from the poor: the Naladiyar's crows leave the carcass and no one asks 'are you well?', Tirumular's dependants turn unloving.
Both describe the poor man estranged from those closest to him; the Kural goes as far as his own mother.
Both say what can never be filled is ended not by filling it but by removing its cause: craving in the Kural, impurity in Tirumular. This depends on reading the pit as desire and not only the belly.
Both treat ties as obstacles to ending births: the Kural asks why one bent on that would keep other ties when even the body is excess, Tirumular calls clinging kin worse than deeds.
Both name the five senses as what must be overcome; the Kural says their domain must be crushed, Tirumular describes the suffering they cause until one turns to the Lord.

211 is a near-repeat of 210: people seek gold to fill the pit, and the pit fills only as impurity goes (அக்குழி தூரும் அழுக்கற்ற வாறே). 210 ends with the same line on the pit filled when impurity is gone, but its remedy is to praise the Lord; 211's is to know the understanding that fills it (அக்குழி தூர்க்கும் அறிவை அறிந்தபின்). Read together, the pair offers worship and knowledge as two routes to one cure.

source_issues: 212: line 4 reads தூர்க்கலு ம், a stray space in தூர்க்கலும்.
